source: MAFF General Directorate of Agriculture, banana cultivation techniques manual, 2019, section IV.1 (watering)
text:
Banana needs a consistent water supply because it is a fast-growing plant with a large pseudostem that stores a lot of water, and because its roots are shallow and cannot draw on deep soil moisture the way a tree crop can. The Chek Pong Moan variety in particular has roots extending to around 50cm and needs frequent watering during dry spells to avoid stress.

Before planting, farmers should confirm they have an adequate water source for the dry season, ideally with access to a pond, stream, or a drip irrigation system, because banana tolerates neither prolonged waterlogging (which suffocates roots) nor drought (which causes leaf damage and yield loss) well. The driest, hottest months (around the dry season and into April) are the highest-risk period: low rainfall combined with high temperature and low humidity at this time can damage leaves, stress the plant, and reduce both yield and fruit quality if watering is neglected.

Common watering methods are furrow/flood irrigation along the rows or sprinkler irrigation; recommended interval is roughly every 3-8 days depending on soil type and season, and farmers are encouraged to check soil moisture at root depth (about one foot down) before deciding whether to water, rather than watering on a fixed schedule regardless of conditions.
